facts.statement: The genus Onchopristis is classified under the authority of Villalobos-Segura, Kriwet, Vullo, Stumpf, Ward, and Underwood in 2021.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Villalobos-Segura, Kriwet, Vullo, Stumpf, Ward, & Underwood, 2021

facts.statement: The genus Onchopristis was originally described by Ernst Stromer in 1917.
facts.quote: authority: Stromer, 1917

facts.statement: In 1905, Émile Haug named the species Gigantichthys numidus based on fragmentary rostral denticles found in Algeria.
facts.quote: In 1905, the French paleontologist Émile Haug named Gigantichthys numidus based on fragmentary rostral denticles from the Continental intercalaire of Algeria

facts.statement: Ernst Stromer assigned the species to the new genus Onchopristis in 1917.
facts.quote: In 1917, Ernst Stromer assigned "G". numidus to a new genus Onchopristis

facts.statement: The species Onchopristis dunklei was named by Charles McNulty, Jr. and Bob Slaughter in 1962.
facts.quote: A second valid species from the Woodbine Formation of Texas, Onchopristis dunklei, was named by Charles McNulty, Jr. and Bob Slaughter in 1962

facts.statement: Some researchers suggest that the two valid species of Onchopristis might actually be a single taxon with morphological variation due to its wide geographical range.
facts.quote: The genus contains two valid species, O. numida and O. dunklei, though some researchers argue that both may be considered a single taxon with variation in morphology caused by a wide geographical range

facts.statement: Onchopristis lived in coastal and river deposits from the Barremian to Cenomanian ages (approximately 125 to 94 million years ago), making it one of the oldest known sclerorhynchoids.
facts.quote: Specimens of Onchopristis have been discovered in coastal and fluvial deposits dated from the Barremian to the Cenomanian ages (~125-94 mya), making this genus one of the oldest known sclerorhynchoids

facts.statement: Onchopristis is an extinct genus of sawskate found in Cretaceous deposits across North Africa, Europe, North America, and possibly South America.
facts.quote: Onchopristis is an extinct genus of sclerorhynchoid, or sawskate, from the Cretaceous of North Africa, Europe, North America, and potentially South America

facts.statement: Specimens of Onchopristis numida suggest a body length between 2.21 and 4.25 meters and a weight between 70 and 150 kilograms.
facts.quote: Specimens of O. numida, IPUW 353500 and IGR 2818, suggest a length estimate of 2.94 - 4.25 m and 2.21 - 3.15 m, respectively; such individuals would have weighed 70 - 150 kg

facts.statement: Onchopristis possessed a long rostrum with large denticles, a feature similar to the 'saws' of modern sawfishes and sawsharks.
facts.quote: Like other sclerorhynchoids, Onchopristis had 'saw', a long rostrum with large denticles, similar to those of sawfishes and sawsharks

facts.statement: The rostral saw of Onchopristis was made of cartilage and was compressed from top to bottom.
facts.quote: The saw, like in those taxa and in other sclerorhynchoids, was cartilaginous and compressed dorsoventrally (from top-to-bottom)

facts.statement: The denticles on the sides of Onchopristis's rostrum were larger than those at the front, with the largest measuring 7 centimeters.
facts.quote: The rostral denticles at the very front of the saw were very small, Those on the sides of the saw were larger with the biggest measuring 7 cm

facts.statement: The skull base (neurocranium) of Onchopristis was rectangular and box-like in shape.
facts.quote: The neurocranium was rectangular in shape and box-like

facts.statement: Onchopristis had a large orbital cavity, or eye socket.
facts.quote: The orbital cavity, or eye socket, is large

facts.statement: The oral teeth of Onchopristis had well-developed cutting edges that extended continuously from the main cusp to the side cusplets.
facts.quote: Known oral teeth all display well-developed cutting edges, extending continuously between the cusp and lateral cusplets

facts.statement: Fossil evidence shows that Spinosaurus preyed on Onchopristis, indicated by rostral denticles found within Spinosaurus jaws in North Africa.
facts.quote: Specimens of Onchopristis have been associated with the jaws of Spinosaurus in North Africa, indicating that Spinosaurus would have preyed upon Onchopristis based on direct evidence of piscivory

facts.statement: Teeth of Spinosaurus and rostral denticles of Onchopristis are found together in a bone bed in the Kem Kem beds of Morocco.
facts.quote: Additionally, the teeth of Spinosaurus and rostral denticles of Onchopristis form a bone bed at one locality in the Kem Kem beds of Morocco (Errachidia Province)

facts.statement: It is debated whether rostral denticles found in Mali belong to Onchopristis numida or are actually cutlassfish fangs.
facts.quote: In 2019, the isolated rostral denticles found in the possible late Maastrichtian-Paleocene strata from Mali were attributed to O. numida, but these specimens more likely represent cutlassfish fangs

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the assignment of a 1.46-meter rostrum and denticles from Egypt's Dakhla Formation to Onchopristis, with some researchers arguing they belong to a different sclerorhynchoid.
facts.quote: In 2024, four fragmentary rostral denticles and an exceptionally large, 1.46 m long rostrum of sclerorhynchoids from the Maastrichtian-aged Dakhla Formation of Egypt were referred to as Onchopristis sp. However, Greenfield (2025) argued that neither of the referred material from the Dakhla Formation can be assigned to Onchopristis

facts.statement: The evolution of the saw-like rostrum in Onchopristis is an example of 'pristification,' a trait that evolved independently multiple times among cartilaginous fish.
facts.quote: This feature was the result of convergent evolution, and its repeated evolution among chondrichthyans has been dubbed 'pristification'

facts.statement: The genus Onchopristis was described by Stromer in 1917.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Stromer, 1917

facts.statement: Onchopristis is classified within the family Pristidae.
facts.quote: familia: Pristidae

facts.statement: The Paleobiology Database classifies Onchopristis as a member of the family Sclerorhynchidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Sclerorhynchidae

facts.statement: Onchopristis lived during the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Cretácico Superior

facts.statement: Fossils of Onchopristis date from the Barremian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 125.77 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Maastrichtian (125.77 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Onchopristis had a long, paddle-shaped snout lined on both sides with hook-shaped barbed teeth.
facts.quote: Tenía un alargado hocico en forma de pala alineado en ambos lados con dientes barbados en forma de gancho.

facts.statement: Fully developed Onchopristis could reach a length of about 10 meters.
facts.quote: Era muy grande, llegando a medir unos 10 metros de longitud cuando estaba completamente desarrollado.

facts.statement: Females were likely larger than males and could weigh between 1 and 1.5 tonnes.
facts.quote: Probablemente las hembras serían mayores que los machos, y pesarían entre 1 - 1.5 toneladas.

facts.statement: The rostrum and snout measured nearly 3 meters in length and featured hook-like teeth.
facts.quote: El rostrum y hocico, medía cerca de 3 metros de largo, con dientes como garfios.

facts.statement: The snout likely possessed electroreceptors to detect prey underwater, similar to modern sharks.
facts.quote: El rostro muy probablemente debió haber poseído electrorreceptores, para poder detectar su comida bajo el agua como los tiburones modernos.

facts.statement: Onchopristis may have raked river beds to find and devour its prey.
facts.quote: Onchopristis puede haber rastrillado el lecho de los ríos para hallar y luego devorar a sus presas.

facts.statement: Remains of Onchopristis have been found in North America, South America, North Africa, and New Zealand.
facts.quote: conocido a partir de restos descubiertos en América del Norte, América del Sur, África del Norte y Nueva Zelanda.

facts.statement: Onchopristis appeared in the first episode of the British documentary Planet Dinosaur.
facts.quote: Onchopristis apareció en el primer capítulo del documental británico Planet Dinosaur.

facts.statement: In the documentary Planet Dinosaur, Onchopristis is depicted as anadromous, spawning in rivers and being preyed upon by the dinosaur Spinosaurus.
facts.quote: Aquí se lo representa siendo anádromo, reproduciéndose en ríos al igual que el salmón actual, y siendo depredado por el dinosaurio Spinosaurus.
